text: The four consumed surfaces of the appeal are read as non-blocking and built against their fakes: the D7.4 approval of rwb-decision on a contract story of an earlier wave (a C dependency that never blocks), the rwb-case case read and route facts on a published case contract whose operation name stays the placeholder, the rwb-partner firm instruction request on a published partner contract whose operation name stays the placeholder, and the LOV-LEGAL-TYPE and LOV-LEGAL-STATUS values on the reference data of rwb-case through the platform client library. The metadata rows of both slices are kept exactly as the plan gives them, with Contract, Integration and External dependencies None, and the two platform contracts of the pattern set (RWB-PLT-E1027-CON and RWB-PLT-N001-CON) stay in the app story's build list.
why: The plan's dependency rows for this key name no contract, integration or external dependency while the story must reach the approval, the case and the firm, and DP-07 and DP-08 are not in its pattern set; inventing a C or H row would change the plan's build sequence, and calling another service's table directly would break DP-01 and DP-05. Recording the four as consumed and faked keeps the metadata as the plan gives it and still lets the story start on Day 1.

text: Neither the appeal grounds nor the appeal window end is stored in rwb_litigation: the grounds travel in the inputs reference of the decision record together with the document of rwb-document that carries them, and the window end is a durable timer of LitigationWorkflow on the case route state. No column, no element and no migration is added for either, and a source that later names a column is a new major version of the DDL template and of the contract.
why: Legacy AC1 requires the grounds to be recorded, but TSD S4 T3.1 gives fourteen columns of legal_action and none is a grounds column, the FSD field catalog of A2.14.3.2 gives eight and none is the grounds either, and the window end is a rule condition of R-LIT-46 with no field anywhere; inventing a column would create a data element no owner approved and would fix the invented name for every later legal action, while refusing to record the grounds at all would drop a legacy criterion.

text: The appeal legal action takes only values of LOV-LEGAL-STATUS: OPEN from the moment the appeal window opens and the decision record is written, FILED when the firm confirms the filing, and WITHDRAWN when the approver declines under R-LIT-49 or the appeal is not pursued. The states JUDGMENT_DISMISSED, APPEAL_DECISION, APPEAL_FILED, IN_HEARING and TO_WRITE_OFF are case route states of rwb-case, announced by this service and never written on the row. The appeal decision and its reason live on the decision record, because no list value names them.
why: The two vocabularies are easy to confuse and a wrong reading would either fork LOV-LEGAL-STATUS with case states or leave the row in a status that no list allows; the six list values do not name a decided or a declined appeal, and moving the case is not this service's write. Recording the ruling keeps the row inside the published list and keeps the case route state with its owner while the decision stays traceable.

text: The appeal window length and the filing deadline of R-LIT-47 are versioned reference rows read with their version in force, held as durable timers of LitigationWorkflow, and their content is carried as the placeholder in both stories. No value is written in code and no figure is taken from another module's clock.
why: The rules turn on both lengths and no source read for this key states either: the rule table gives service levels only, legal_action has no window or deadline column, and the FSD validation and business rules of A2.14 give no interval. Guessing a figure would put a legal deadline into code and would be wrong for at least one court and one product group, and hard-coding the value would break BR-S4-014.
